title: The Genetic Landscape of Alzheimer’s Disease: Mechanisms, Risk Factors, and the Emerging Role of Brain-Derived Cell-Free DNA
content: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that erodes memory, cognition, and behavior. Its enormous social and economic costs underscore the need for improved early detection and individualized treatment strategies. Early-onset AD, which manifests before the age of 65, can be due to highly penetrant rare mutations in genes such as APP, PSEN1, PSEN2, and MAPT. Late-onset AD is multifactorial with polygenic predisposition defined by many risk loci, the most firmly established of which is the APOE ε4 allele. A further contributor to late-onset disease is the accumulation of somatic mutations in the aging brain, which can be detected in brain-derived cell-free DNA (bd cfDNA) recoverable from blood. This narrative review surveys the neuropathological hallmarks, pathogenic mechanisms, risk factors and the genetic basis of AD placing emphasis on bd cfDNA. Bd cf DNA is released in neuronal death and can pass the compromised blood-brain barrier. It can reach detectable amounts and shows differences in size, methylation profile and even sequence from the background cell-free DNA. These facts point to the need for more comprehensive analyses of brain-derived cell free DNA in favor of its potential as a blood biomarker for prevention, early-diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease.
